raw_evidence.label: Origin: Te Papa & Australasian Seabird Mapping Scheme
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is a digitization of paper logbooks held at Te Papa Tongarewa, the Museum of New Zealand, covering at-sea seabird observations from 1969 to 1990 in New Zealand and Australian waters (the Tasman Sea region). Counts followed the Australasian Seabird Mapping Scheme (ASMS) protocol: from a moving or stationary ship, an observer records every bird seen during a 10-minute window, with location, species, behaviour, and weather. The ASMS was a long-running citizen-science program aimed at producing the first systematic at-sea distribution maps for Southern Hemisphere seabirds, and Te Papa is the curating institution for the New Zealand portion of the archive. Each record is one 10-minute census; the project is the deepest publicly available ship-based seabird record for this region for the late 20th century.

raw_evidence.label: Origin: Te Papa & Australasian Seabird Mapping Scheme
raw_evidence.content: The dataset is a digitization of paper logbooks held at Te Papa Tongarewa, the Museum of New Zealand, covering at-sea seabird observations from 1969 to 1990 in New Zealand and Australian waters (the Tasman Sea region). Counts followed the Australasian Seabird Mapping Scheme (ASMS) protocol: from a moving or stationary ship, an observer records every bird seen during a 10-minute window, with location, species, behaviour, and weather. The ASMS was a long-running citizen-science program aimed at producing the first systematic at-sea distribution maps for Southern Hemisphere seabirds, and Te Papa is the curating institution for the New Zealand portion of the archive. Each record is one 10-minute census; the project is the deepest publicly available ship-based seabird record for this region for the late 20th century.

raw_evidence.label: The hand-recorded log: a data quality time capsule
raw_evidence.content: Every entry was written by hand by an observer on a ship between 1969 and 1990, then later transcribed and standardised by Te Papa staff. The free-text species_common_name column was the original log entry; the structured columns (species_scientific_name, age, plumage_phase, sex) were derived afterwards. This means downstream values are only as good as the transcription, and the curating team has flagged that some entries can not be resolved to a single species (logged as a slash-separated 'aggregate'). The sentinel values 99999 (counts > 100,000) and the special string '[NO BIRDS RECORDED]' (now NA in species_common_name) are critical to handle correctly — analysts who treat 99999 as a real count will get wildly wrong means.

raw_evidence.label: Top species by total birds counted: shearwaters dwarf albatrosses
raw_evidence.content: Ranking by sum of birds counted (excluding the six 99,999 sentinels) flips the picture: short-tailed shearwater accounts for 482,558 of the 1,342,219 birds counted across the program (36% of all birds), with prion (unidentified) at 226,500 and sooty shearwater at 174,329. Albatrosses, which dominate by record count, do not even reach the top 15 by individuals: they are seen often but in small flocks, while shearwaters are seen less often but in massive feeding aggregations of thousands.

raw_evidence.label: Beaufort and sea-state context
raw_evidence.content: Wind and sea state are not just colour — they shape what an observer can see. At Beaufort 6+ (gale and above) whitecaps, spray and ship motion all reduce detection. Conversely, dynamic-soaring albatrosses are essentially absent in flat-calm Beaufort 0 conditions because they cannot soar without wind. The Beaufort scale (0 calm to 12 hurricane) and the 0–6 sea-state scale are joined to ship records and let us ask whether seabird counts vary with weather — but with the caveat that detection probability and bird behaviour move in opposite directions as wind rises.

raw_evidence.label: Median count is steady from breeze to gale
raw_evidence.content: Median birds-per-census stays remarkably stable across the breeze range: 6 at calm, 7 at light air, 8 at Beaufort 2-4 and 6, 9 at fresh breeze, near gale, and strong gale, then 10 at gale. Mean counts are noisier because of giant flocks: 287.6 mean at Beaufort 0 (driven by a few huge static-water counts), 226.1 at Beaufort 1, dropping to 52.6-135 in the breeze range. The hurricane census (n=1) recorded zero birds. Overall, weather alone is a poor predictor of how many birds an observer recorded.
